title: Gesta Hungarorum (Anonymus)
fact_summary: The Deeds of the Hungarians, by a notary known only as Anonymus: the oldest surviving Hungarian chronicle, written about three hundred years after the events it describes.

claims.text: Its translator calls it “the oldest extant chronicle of the history of the Hungarians”, surviving in a single manuscript of 24 leaves, first noted near Innsbruck in the seventeenth century, moved to Vienna in 1665 and to Budapest in 1928, and first printed in 1746.
claims.certainty_reason: The translator's account in a scholarly introduction; the manuscript's history has not been checked elsewhere.

claims.text: The translator says of the author: “The most that can be said about him is that his name began with a P.”
The author says he writes because it would be unfitting for the Hungarians to learn of their origins from “the gabbling song of minstrels”.
claims.certainty_reason: This records what the source says, read in Martyn Rady's English translation in the open copy linked under Sources. The Latin has not been compared.

claims.text: The work is “at best an attempt to project contemporary conditions backwards”: its picture of who held power north of the Danube in the late ninth century “is not supported by any other account”.
claims.certainty_reason: The translator's judgement; other scholars' views have not been read.

claims.text: Readings of the Gesta were used in the twentieth century “to buttress historical claims to territories”.
claims.certainty_reason: The translator's account of how the text has been used.

open_questions.text: Which parts of the Gesta can be checked against earlier sources, and which stand alone?

review.note: Checked by Claude against open copies of every source. Marc spot-checks a sample.
